fields.explanation:
Full source assumes the relation direct-image map is surjective. Of the original three witnesses, witness3 satisfies this entire premise and also refutes the displayed singleton exclusion. Keep originalS={0,1,2},T={0,1}, relation rows{0},{1},{0,1}. Its powerset image is onto, but row2 branches and both singleton images exist. Mathlib SetRel.image is proved surjective for every target subset, with actual non-single-valued relation. Original smaller diagnostic examples are not used to omit surjectivity.

R^-> preserves unions, so surjectivity forces every {y} to be a union of sets R(x), hence some R(x) = {y}; y |-> x_y is injective, and only when S is finite with |S| = |T| does it exhaust S and forbid a branching x.
fields.flaw: In case (2) (some x is related by R to two distinct y_1 != y_2), the proof asserts that neither {y_1} nor {y_2} can lie in the range of R^-> , and concludes from this that R^-> cannot be a surjection.
fields.problem:
Title: Surjection Induced by Powerset is Induced by Surjection

Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a [[Definition:Relation|relation]].

Let $\RR^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T$ be the [[Definition:Direct Image Mapping of Relation|direct image mapping]] $\RR$.

Let $\RR^\to$ be a [[Definition:Surjection|surjection]].

Let $X = \Preimg \RR$, that is, the [[Definition:Preimage of Relation|preimage]] of $\RR$.

Then $\RR {\restriction_X} \subseteq X \times T$, that is, the [[Definition:Restriction of Relation|restriction of $\RR$ to $X$]], is a [[Definition:Surjection|surjection]].
fields.source_context:
0012 | 
0013 | So we see that $\RR^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T$ is not a [[Definition:Surjection|surjection]].
0014 | 
0015 | Now, suppose $\RR {\restriction_X} \subseteq X \times T$ is not even a [[Definition:Mapping|mapping]].
0016 | 
0017 | This could happen, according to the definition of a [[Definition:Mapping|mapping]], in one of two ways:
0018 | 
0019 | :$(1): \quad \exists x \in X: \neg \exists y \in T: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR$
0020 | :$(2): \quad \exists x \in S: \tuple {x, y_1} \in \RR \land \tuple {x, y_2} \in \RR: y_1 \ne y_2$
0021 | 
0022 | Because $X$ is already the [[Definition:Preimage of Relation|preimage of $\RR$]], the first of these cannot happen here.
0023 | 
0024 | For the second, it can be seen that neither $\set {y_1}$ nor $\set {y_2}$ can be in $\Rng {\map {\RR^\to} {\powerset S} }$.
0025 | 
0026 | Therefore $\RR^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T$ can not be a [[Definition:Surjection|surjection]].
0027 | 
0028 | Thus, by the [[Rule of Transposition]], the result follows.
0029 | {{qed}}
0030 | 
0031 | [[Category:Surjections]]
0032 | [[Category:Direct Image Mappings]]
fields.witness:
The asserted lemma is FALSE, refuted by a 3-pair relation on a 2-element set; a 4-pair endorelation on a 3-element set refutes BOTH halves at once; and a 4-pair relation with S != T even refutes the downstream "cannot be a surjection" conclusion.

WITNESS 1 (smallest; refutes the sentence as literally written).
  S = T = {0,1},  R = {(0,0), (1,0), (1,1)}, i.e. R(0) = {0}, R(1) = {0,1}.
  Case (2) hypothesis holds: x = 1 is R-related to y_1 = 0 and y_2 = 1, and y_1 != y_2.
  Direct image mapping R^->(A) = union_{x in A} R(x):
    R^->({}) = {},  R^->({0}) = {0},  R^->({1}) = {0,1},  R^->({0,1}) = {0,1}.
  Rng(R^->) = { {}, {0}, {0,1} }.
  Claim says {y_1} = {0} is NOT in Rng(R^->); here A = {0} gives R^->(A) = {0}, so {0} IS in Rng(R^->).

WITNESS 2 (endorelation, refutes BOTH conjuncts simultaneously; hand-verified separately).
  S = T = {0,1,2},  R = {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (2,1)}, i.e. R(0) = {0,1}, R(1) = {0}, R(2) = {1}.
  Case (2) holds: x = 0 branches to y_1 = 0 and y_2 = 1.
  Rng(R^->) = { {}, {0}, {1}, {0,1} }.
  A = {1} gives R^->(A) = {0} = {y_1}; A = {2} gives R^->(A) = {1} = {y_2}.
  Claim says neither singleton can be in the range; here BOTH are.

WITNESS 3 (refutes the CONCLUSION itself when the relation is heterogeneous, S != T).
  S = {0,1,2}, T = {0,1},  R = {(0,0), (1,1), (2,0), (2,1)}: R(0) = {0}, R(1) = {1}, R(2) = {0,1}.
  Case (2) holds: x = 2 branches to y_1 = 0, y_2 = 1.
  Rng(R^->) = { {}, {0}, {1}, {0,1} } = P(T); |Rng(R^->)| = 4 = |P(T)| = 4.
  Claim says R^-> "cannot be a surjection"; here R^-> IS a surjection onto P(T).
